Mobile Game Landscape: Mobile gaming is the largest segment of the games industry. Phones and tablets offer unique constraints: touch input, limited battery, thermal throttling, fragmented hardware, and interrupt-driven usage (calls, notifications). Success requires designing for short sessions, efficient resource use, and broad device compatibility. The major engines (Unity, Unreal, Godot) all support mobile export with platform-specific optimizations.
Choosing a Mobile Engine: Unity dominates mobile with 60%+ market share — excellent cross-platform support, massive asset store, and C# scripting. Unreal Engine targets high-end mobile with stunning visuals but heavier APK sizes and higher device requirements. Godot is lightweight, open-source, and exports to Android/iOS with minimal overhead but a smaller mobile community. For 2D mobile games, Godot or Unity 2D are great choices. For 3D, Unity balances quality and performance; Unreal excels on flagship devices.
Mobile Build Pipeline: Building for mobile involves multiple steps: code compilation, asset compression, texture format conversion (ETC2 for Android, PVRTC/ASTC for iOS), architecture-specific binaries (ARM64, ARMv7), and final packaging. Unity uses the Build Settings window or command-line builds. Android produces APK or AAB (Android App Bundle). iOS produces IPA via Xcode. Each platform requires specific SDKs, NDKs, and provisioning profiles.

Touch Events & Multi-Touch: Mobile input is fundamentally different from mouse/keyboard. Touch events provide position, phase (began/moved/ended/cancelled), and a unique finger ID for multi-touch. The screen is a direct manipulation surface — what you touch is what you interact with. Input latency on mobile typically ranges from 40-100ms. Always handle the cancelled phase (system interrupts like calls). Maximum simultaneous touches varies from 5-10 depending on device.
Gesture Recognition: Common mobile gestures: tap, double-tap, long-press, swipe, pinch-to-zoom, rotate, drag, flick. Implement gesture recognizers that track touch state over time. A tap is a brief touch/release within a distance threshold (usually < 10px) and time threshold (< 300ms). A swipe requires minimum velocity and distance. Pinch tracks two touch points' distance changes. Use dead zones (small ignored movements) to prevent jitter from noisy touch input.
Virtual Joysticks & Buttons: Virtual controls overlay the screen with touch zones mapped to game actions. Joysticks track a touch point within a radius — the normalized offset from center becomes the input vector. Buttons trigger on touch began within their rect. Place controls in the lower screen thirds (thumb zones) and avoid the notch/camera cutout area. Consider configurable layouts for accessibility. Scale controls relative to screen resolution and aspect ratio.
Haptic Feedback: Haptic feedback improves immersion and confirms actions. Android uses VibrationEffect with amplitude control. iOS uses UIImpactFeedbackGenerator, UINotificationFeedbackGenerator, and UISelectionFeedbackGenerator for different haptic patterns. Unity's Handheld.Vibrate() provides basic support; plugins like Lofelt provide advanced haptic design. Use haptics sparingly — overuse drains battery and annoys players. Respect system-level haptic settings.

Battery & Thermal Optimization: Mobile devices throttle performance when overheating. CPU/GPU intensive tasks, background networking, and inefficient rendering drain battery. Profile thermal impact: measure temperature rise per operation. Key strategies: reduce CPU frame time (< 16ms for 60fps), minimize GPU overdraw, batch draw calls (< 100), use efficient physics (fewer colliders, simpler shapes), and reduce WiFi/cellular polling. iOS reports thermal state via ProcessInfo.thermalState. Android monitors via PowerManager.
การจัดการหน่วยความจำ: Mobile has limited RAM (2-8GB shared with OS). Texture memory is the biggest consumer: a 2048x2048 RGBA texture = 16MB. Android's onTrimMemory() warns of impending kill. iOS issues memory warnings via didReceiveMemoryWarning. Load assets progressively, unload unused scenes, use mipmaps (saves ~33% GPU memory), and compress textures (ETC2/ASTC). Avoid large contiguous allocations — they fragment the heap. Pool and reuse objects instead of allocate/free cycles.
Adaptive Quality Scaling: Device capabilities vary enormously. Measure GPU fill rate, RAM, and screen resolution at startup, then set quality tiers. Use a quality profile that adjusts: shadow resolution, anti-aliasing, post-processing, texture resolution, draw distance, particle count, and LOD bias. Re-evaluate periodically and when thermal state changes. Unity's QualitySettings and Godot's OS methods support runtime quality changes.
Asset Bundles & Streaming: Mobile games must manage download size and memory. Asset bundles (Unity) or resource packs (Godot) let you split content into on-demand chunks. Initial download should be under 150MB. Stream additional levels, textures, and audio on demand. Use addressable assets for runtime loading with reference counting. Cache downloaded bundles to device storage. Prioritize essential assets (first level, UI) and defer high-res textures and later levels. Use LZ4 compression for faster runtime decompression.

Responsive Layout System: Mobile screens range from 320x480 (old budget) to 1440x3040 (flagship). Use anchor-based layouts that scale relative to screen edges. Avoid absolute pixel positions. Calculate UI scale based on reference resolution (typically 1080p for mobile). Handle safe areas (notch, camera cutout, status bar, gesture bar). Unity's Canvas Scaler with 'Scale With Screen Size' handles most cases. For Godot, use Control nodes with anchors. Always test on a variety of screen sizes.
Mobile UX Patterns for Games: Mobile games thrive on simplicity: short sessions (3-5 minutes), clear goals, immediate feedback. Thumb zones: top = less reachable (menus, info), bottom = thumb-friendly (actions, navigation). Avoid right-edge swipe (system gesture conflict on iOS). Use touch-friendly targets (minimum 44x44pt, ideally 48x48pt). Provide visual feedback on touch (press state, animation). Use onboarding tutorials that respect player agency — let them skip or replay.
Interruptions & State Persistence: Mobile games are frequently interrupted: incoming calls, notifications, app switcher, low battery. Save game state aggressively — on every significant action, not just on graceful exit. Handle OnApplicationPause (Unity) or _notification() with NOTIFICATION_APPLICATION_PAUSED (Godot). Serialize critical state (player position, score, inventory, quest progress) to persistent storage. Use auto-save with a cooldown (every 30s or on checkpoint). On resume, restore state seamlessly without reloading the entire scene.

Handling Mobile Network Conditions: Mobile networks are unreliable: high latency (100-500ms cellular), packet loss, IP address changes, and frequent disconnections (tunnels, elevators). Design for offline-first with sync-on-reconnect. Use TCP for reliable state updates and UDP for real-time gameplay with interpolation/extrapolation. Implement reconnection with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...). Detect connection type (WiFi vs cellular) to adjust data usage. Respect metered connections — offer low-data mode.
Offline Mode & Sync: Offline-first architecture lets players continue without connectivity. Queue actions locally, sync when online. Use a local database (SQLite via Unity's SQLite plugin, or IndexedDB for web). Track a sync version per record to resolve conflicts. Last-write-wins works for simple data; CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) for complex multiplayer. Show clear indicators for online/offline state. Never block gameplay waiting for network — use optimistic updates and reconcile later.
Real-Time Multiplayer on Mobile: Mobile real-time multiplayer faces latency, connection drops, and data costs. Use UDP with reliability layers (like ENET or KCP) for fast-paced games. Implement client-side prediction and server reconciliation. For turn-based games, use WebSocket with JSON payloads. Photon, Mirror (Unity), and Nakama are popular mobile netcode solutions. Matchmaking should consider ping (prefer < 100ms), skill rating, and platform (iOS vs Android cross-play). Use delta compression to minimize data per packet.

Ads Integration: Mobile ads come in several formats: banner (static, low eCPM), interstitial (full-screen between levels, medium eCPM), rewarded video (player opts in for reward, highest eCPM), and native (integrated into UI). Major networks: AdMob (Google), Unity Ads, AppLovin, ironSource. Mediation platforms (AdMob Mediation, ironSource) maximize fill rate by routing to the highest-paying network. Implement ad frequency capping (max 3 interstitials per 10 minutes). Never show ads during gameplay — place them at natural breaks (level transitions, menu screens).
In-App Purchases: IAPs include consumables (gems, coins, extra lives), non-consumables (remove ads, full game unlock), and subscriptions (weekly/monthly pass). Apple takes 30% (15% for small businesses under $1M). Google takes 15-30%. Use Unity IAP or a cross-platform purchase library. Always validate receipts server-side to prevent fraud. Implement a store UI that shows prices in local currency. Provide a 'restore purchases' button (required by Apple). Never make the game unplayable without IAP — monetize ethically.
Analytics & Engagement: Track player behavior: session length, retention (D1/D7/D30), conversion rate, average revenue per daily active user (ARPDAU), and funnel analysis (tutorial completion → first purchase → level 5). Use Firebase Analytics, Unity Analytics, or GameAnalytics. Implement event tracking with consistent naming: level_start, level_complete, iap_purchase. Send push notifications for re-engagement (daily rewards, new content). Use A/B testing for pricing and feature changes. Respect GDPR/CCPA privacy requirements.

GPU Architecture for Mobile: Mobile GPUs use tile-based deferred rendering (TBDR) — they split the frame into tiles (typically 16x16 or 32x32), process geometry per tile, then render. This differs from desktop immediate-mode GPUs. Key implications: minimize overdraw (tiles pay for hidden pixels), use fewer but larger triangles, batch draw calls, avoid alpha blending (forces multiple passes), and use power-of-two textures. Apple GPUs (A-series) are TBDR; Qualcomm Adreno uses a hybrid approach. Mali GPUs (ARM) are also tile-based.
Texture Compression & Formats: Mobile texture formats: ETC2 (mandatory for OpenGL ES 3.0+ Android), ASTC (universal, best quality, supported by iOS 9+/Android 10+), PVRTC (legacy iOS), and ETC1 (old Android, no alpha). ASTC is preferred — it offers flexible bitrates (4-12 bpp) and good quality. Always generate mipmaps for 3D scenes (saves GPU memory bandwidth). Compress GUI textures too — uncompressed RGBA at 1080p = 8MB per full-screen texture. Use sprite atlases to batch UI draw calls.
Shader Optimization for Mobile: Mobile shaders are constrained by instruction count (32-128 instructions), limited texture samples (8-16), and no dynamic branching on many GPUs. Use the #pragma target 3.0 minimum. Reduce precision: fixed (11-bit) for colors, half for positions/UVs, float only when necessary. Avoid pow, exp, log, sin, cos in fragment shaders (use lookup textures). Precompute lighting in vertex shaders. Use fewer lights — ideally 1 directional + 0-1 point lights. Bake lighting into lightmaps when possible.

Audio Formats & Compression: OGG uses Vorbis compression for music (good quality/size), MP3 is universally supported but slightly older, AAC offers better quality than MP3 at same bitrate, ADPCM is lossless-ish and fast for short SFX. On mobile, Unity's AudioImporter lets you choose compressed (OGG) for long clips vs ADPCM for short SFX to balance memory vs CPU decode cost. Streaming loads from disk instead of RAM but adds I/O overhead.
Spatial Audio on Mobile: Ambisonics captures full-sphere surround sound; HRTF filters simulate 3D direction using head-related transfer functions. iOS spatial audio leverages AirPods motion tracking for fixed-position sounds. Android spatial audio uses Google's Resonance Audio or Oboe. FMOD and Wwise provide cross-platform spatial audio with occlusion, reverb zones, and dynamic mixing channels tuned for mobile CPU budgets.
Audio Latency & Optimization: iOS audio latency is minimized via AVAudioSession with category .playAndRecord and preferredIOBufferDuration (e.g. 0.005). Android uses Oboe or AAudio for low-latency paths. Unity's AudioMixer groups duck music under SFX, apply DSP effects (low-pass on pause), and profile via Audio Profiler. Streaming avoids loading entire clips into RAM but can stutter if I/O spikes; preload short clips as CompressedInMemory.

ARCore & ARKit Basics: ARCore (Android) and ARKit (iOS) enable motion tracking, environmental understanding, and light estimation. ARCore uses visual-inertial odometry (VIO) — fusing camera imagery with IMU data. ARKit uses Visual Inertial Odometry + scene reconstruction with LiDAR on Pro devices. Both provide: plane detection (horizontal/vertical), point clouds, image tracking, object detection (ARKit 3+), and face tracking. Unity AR Foundation abstracts both APIs into a single workflow. Anchor virtual content to real-world positions using trackables.
AR Game Design Patterns: AR games blend digital content with the real world. Design principles: surface alignment (content sits on tables/floors), scale matters (virtual objects should look physically sized), occlusion (hide objects behind real walls — LiDAR helps), lighting consistency (match virtual light to real environment), and persistent anchors (save object positions across sessions). User education is critical — show onboarding that demonstrates scanning surfaces and moving around. Handle low-light conditions gracefully (ARKit provides light estimation). Always provide a non-AR fallback mode.

Core ML & ML Kit: Apple Core ML converts models from PyTorch/TF via coremltools for on-device inference — image classification (MobileNet), object detection (YOLO), pose estimation (OpenPose). Google ML Kit provides ready-to-use APIs for text recognition, face detection, barcode scanning, and pose detection with no custom model needed. In mobile games, use these for photo-based character creators, AR overlays, or cheater detection via screen analysis.
Unity Sentis: Unity Sentis runs ONNX neural networks directly in Unity on mobile GPUs via compute shaders. Load a .sentis model asset, create a Worker (GPUCompute or CPUShader), pass input tensors via TensorFloat, execute inference, and read output tensors. Use cases: real-time pose detection for avatar mirroring, style transfer for visual effects, or AI-driven NPC behavior without server calls.
Model Optimization: Quantization reduces model size and speeds inference: FP16 halves size with minimal accuracy loss, INT8 is 4x smaller but needs calibration. Pruning removes near-zero weights. Core ML conversion uses coremltools with ct.quantize_weights(). TFLite supports dynamic range, FP16, and INT8 quantization. For mobile games, prefer FP16 quantized models (<10MB) to stay under app store limits and hit 30fps inference.

Game Controller Support: MFi (Made for iPhone) controllers, Xbox Wireless, and PlayStation DualShock/DualSense pair via Bluetooth. Unity's Input System auto-detects controllers and maps to common layouts (left stick = Vector2, A/B/X/Y = button). Use Gamepad.current to poll and InputAction bindings for cross-platform prompts; detect device type to switch glyphs (e.g. 'A' on Xbox vs 'X' on PlayStation).
Gyroscope & Motion Sensors: Accelerometer measures linear acceleration (g-force), gyroscope measures angular rotation rate, magnetometer acts as digital compass. Unity's Input.gyro gives attitude as a Quaternion for tilt steering (racing games), userAcceleration for step counting, and rotationRate for camera look. Must enable Input.gyro.enabled and typically set Input.compensateSensors = true for screen orientation.
Foldable & Adaptive Screens: Foldable devices (Samsung Galaxy Z Fold, Pixel Fold) require handling screen continuity (activity recreates on fold), hinge angle sensor (half-fold mode for laptop-style gameplay), and display cutout (notch/punch-hole) insets. Samsung DeX and multi-window mean the game must handle arbitrary aspect ratios. Unity's Screen.safeArea gives the non-cutout rect; use OnApplicationFocus or ScreenOrientation changes to relayout.

String Management: Use .po/.json/.resx files for string storage. Unity Localization package provides StringTable assets and LocalizedString variables. Plural rules handle locale-specific forms via Smart Strings. Format strings with {0} placeholders and pass variables at runtime. Set locale from system language or player preference.
RTL & Complex Scripts: Arabic and Hebrew require right-to-left text rendering. TextMeshPro provides the RTL Editor for correct shaping of Arabic/Persian/Urdu. Hindi uses Devanagari script with complex ligatures — TMP handles OpenType shaping. CJK (Chinese, Japanese, Korean) text needs appropriate fallback fonts assigned in TMP Font Asset. Set text direction via TMP_Text.isRightToLeft. Build fallback chain fonts for missing glyphs.
Cultural Adaptation: Adapt content for regional sensitivity — avoid offensive imagery, flags, or political symbols. Format dates per culture: en-US uses MM/dd/yyyy, most EU uses dd/MM/yyyy. Format currency with ISO 4217 codes and locale-aware symbols ($, Euro, Yen). Set regional pricing tiers (e.g., India, Brazil, Turkey have different purchasing power). Pseudolocalization wraps strings with accents to test layout expansion.

Firebase Cloud Messaging: FCM sends push notifications via Firebase. On Android 8+ you must register notification channels with importance levels. Data messages (onMessageReceived in background) vs notification messages (auto-displayed). Manage instance tokens for targeted push; subscribe to topics for group broadcasts. Unity Firebase SDK handles token registration and message forwarding to the game object.
Apple Push Notification Service: APNs delivers notifications to iOS devices via device tokens. Implement UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate to handle incoming pushes. Notification Content Extensions allow custom UI within notification banners. Define notification categories with actions (accept/decline/snooze). Rich media attachments include images, video, and audio in the notification payload.
Deep Linking: Android App Links (verified HTTP intents) and iOS Universal Links open your app directly from URLs. Deferred deep linking attributes installs: user clicks a link before installing, then gets routed to the correct content post-install. Firebase Dynamic Links handle this cross-platform. Handle incoming links at runtime by parsing query parameters and navigating to the relevant screen.

Google Play Games Services: GPGS v2 for Unity provides sign-in, achievements, leaderboards, and Saved Games. Authenticate via PlayGamesPlatform.Instance.Authenticate. Report achievements incrementally or unlock them. Submit scores to leaderboards. Saved Games use ISavedGameClient with conflict resolution. Real-time multiplayer sends reliable/unreliable messages. Player Stats API returns session metrics.
Apple Game Center: GKLocalPlayer.local.authenticateHandler triggers the sign-in dialog. Report scores via GKLeaderboard and achievements via GKAchievement. Real-time matchmaking uses GKMatchRequest and GKMatchmaker; turn-based matches use GKTurnBasedMatch. Listen for player state changes and match events. Leaderboard and achievement IDs must match App Store Connect configuration.
Cross-Platform Social Features: Abstract social services behind a platform-agnostic interface so game code never calls GPGS or Game Center directly. The abstraction exposes sign-in, achievements, leaderboards, cloud saves, friend lists, and invites. Each platform (Google, Apple) implements the interface. The game logic calls the singleton SocialManager, making porting to new platforms trivial.

Battle Pass & Season Pass Design: A battle pass has tiers (50-100 levels) each requiring set XP. Free track gives basic rewards; premium track (one-time purchase per season) adds exclusive skins, currency, and items. FOMO (fear of missing out) drives engagement as season-exclusive content disappears. Analytics track pass completion rate, tier drop-off, and average XP earned per day to tune progression.
Virtual Economy Balancing: Define soft currency (gold, coins) earned via gameplay and hard currency (gems) from purchases. Premium currency bridges free and paid. Inflation occurs when too much currency enters the system — sinks (upgrade costs, cosmetics) drain it; faucets (quest rewards, daily login) inject it. Balance sinks vs faucets per player segment. Price virtual goods based on perceived value.
Subscription Models: Apple auto-renewable subscriptions use StoreKit 2 with SKProduct. Periods: weekly, monthly, yearly. Introductory pricing (free trial, discounted period) increases conversion. Subscription groups allow users to subscribe to one of several options. Track retention via renewal rate and churn. Offer subscriber-only perks (daily bonus multiplier, exclusive items, no ads).

Code Obfuscation & Tamper Protection: Protect your Unity game from reverse engineering by applying ProGuard/R8 rules to strip unused code and obfuscate managed assemblies. Use IL2CPP over Mono to convert C# to C++ before native compilation, making memory inspection far more difficult. Compute runtime integrity checks via SHA256, and detect rooted/jailbroken devices by checking for common binary paths and su binaries.
Network Security: Implement SSL pinning to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks by embedding the server certificate or public key hash directly in the client. On Android use OkHttp's CertificatePinner; on iOS implement URLSession didReceiveChallenge to validate the server trust against a known key. Encrypt payloads with AES-GCM before sending, add timestamps and nonces to prevent replay attacks.
Anti-Cheat for Mobile Games: Detect memory scanners by checking for suspicious process maps. Guard against speed hacks by comparing deltaTime against wall-clock time across multiple frames. Detect emulator environments by inspecting Build.FINGERPRINT, Build.HARDWARE, and Build.MODEL on Android. Encrypt and obfuscate memory values at runtime to reduce the attack surface.

GitHub Actions Pipelines: Define reusable YAML workflows that build Unity games for both iOS and Android triggered by pushes, pull requests, or nightly runs. Use matrix strategies to test across device families and Unity versions. Cache the Library folder to cut build times by 50%. Store .ipa and .aab files as workflow artifacts, then deploy to TestFlight or Play Console via Fastlane.

# .github/workflows/unity-mobile.yml
name: Unity Mobile Build
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
jobs:
  build:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        target: [Android, iOS]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: Library
          key: Library-${{ matrix.target }}-${{ hashFiles('Assets/**') }}
      - name: Unity Build
        uses: game-ci/unity-builder@v4
        with:
          targetPlatform: ${{ matrix.target }}
      - name: Upload Artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: Build-${{ matrix.target }}
          path: build/${{ matrix.target }}

Keyword Research & Metadata: Optimize your Google Play title (30 chars), subtitle (30 chars), and short description (80 chars) to include high-volume, low-competition keywords. On iOS the keyword field (100 chars) is comma-separated. Use Sensor Tower, AppTweak, or Google Play Console keyword reports to discover competitor terms. Refresh metadata seasonally and when launching new content.

// Python keyword analysis
import requests

def analyze_keywords(competitor_id, api_key):
    url = f"https://api.apptweak.io/applications/{competitor_id}/keywords.json"
    response = requests.get(url, headers={"X-AppTweak-Key": api_key})
    keywords = response.json()
    scored = [(kw["keyword"], kw["search_volume"] / max(kw["difficulty"], 1)) for kw in keywords]
    scored.sort(key=lambda x: -x[1])
    return [kw for kw, _ in scored[:20]]
Visual Assets: Design an app icon that reads well at small sizes: single bold subject, vibrant colors, no text. Create screenshot templates showcasing top 3-5 gameplay moments, overlaying UI at the bottom third to avoid safe-area clipping. Produce a preview video (15-30s) that loops automatically. Use Google Play Store Listing Experiments to A/B test icons and screenshots. Localize all assets per region.
Ratings & Reviews Management: Prompt users for ratings at natural engagement milestones (level complete, match win, first purchase) using SKStoreReviewController on iOS and In-App Review API on Google Play. Implement a rate limiter (max once per month) and only show on happy paths. Respond to negative reviews within 24 hours. Track rating trends per build version; investigate if dropping below 4.0 stars.

Android Native Plugins: Bridge Unity C# with Android Java/Kotlin code using AndroidJavaClass and AndroidJavaObject to call methods on the JVM. Package your Kotlin code as an AAR with dependencies declared in the Gradle file, then place it in Assets/Plugins/Android/. Extend UnityPlayerActivity or use UnityAndroidApplication to hook into the activity lifecycle. Use UnityPlayer.UnitySendMessage from Java to invoke C# methods on GameObjects.
iOS Native Plugins: Expose Objective-C/Swift functionality to Unity by writing C-style function wrappers in .mm files that Unity's P/Invoke system can call. Declare [DllImport("__Internal")] extern functions in C# and implement in Objective-C using extern "C" linkage. Embed the static library (.a) or framework in Assets/Plugins/iOS/. For Swift interop, create an Obj-C bridging header that wraps your Swift classes.
Plugin Architecture & Lifecycle: Design your native plugin with a singleton manager that initializes once on app start, wires up lifecycle callbacks (OnApplicationPause, OnApplicationQuit), and dispatches events back to the Unity main thread using ConcurrentQueue. Keep a weak reference to the Unity GameObject. Marshal strings and byte arrays carefully across the managed/native boundary. Wrap all native calls in try/catch.

Android Studio & SDK Setup: Android Studio is the official IDE. Install via JetBrains Toolbox or direct download. SDK Manager provides platform SDKs (target Android 14/API 34 minimum), build tools, NDK (for native C/C++ code), and emulator system images. AVD Manager creates virtual devices for testing. The recommended project structure uses Gradle with Kotlin DSL. Key SDK paths: $ANDROID_HOME, NDK in $ANDROID_NDK_HOME. Use SDK command-line tools (sdkmanager) for CI environments.

# Android SDK setup (CI environment)
export ANDROID_HOME=$HOME/Android/Sdk

# Install SDK components
sdkmanager "platforms;android-34"
sdkmanager "build-tools;34.0.0"
sdkmanager "ndk;26.1.10909125"
sdkmanager "emulator"
sdkmanager "system-images;android-34;google_apis;x86_64"

# Create AVD for testing
echo no | avdmanager create avd \
  -n test_device \
  -k "system-images;android-34;google_apis;x86_64" \
  -d pixel_6

# Build from command line
./gradlew assembleDebug

# Install to connected device
./gradlew installDebug
Android Game Manifest & Permissions: The AndroidManifest.xml configures your game: screen orientation (landscape or portrait), hardware features (android.hardware.touchscreen required), permissions (vibrate, internet, wake lock), and Google Play Services. For games, set android:hardwareAccelerated="true", disable screenshots in secure contexts, and use immersive mode to hide system UI. Declare required OpenGL ES version. For Unity, the manifest is auto-generated; overlay it via Plugins/Android/AndroidManifest.xml.

<!-- AndroidManifest.xml for Unity game -->
<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    package="com.yourcompany.yourgame">
    
    <uses-feature android:name="android.hardware.touchscreen" 
        android:required="true" />
    <uses-feature android:glEsVersion="0x00030000" 
        android:required="true" />
    
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.VIBRATE" />
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE" />
    
    <application android:label="My Game"
        android:hardwareAccelerated="true"
        android:allowBackup="false"
        android:largeHeap="true"
        android:theme="@android:style/Theme.NoTitleBar.Fullscreen">
        
        <activity android:name="com.unity3d.player.UnityPlayerActivity"
            android:screenOrientation="sensorLandscape"
            android:configChanges="orientation|keyboardHidden|screenSize"
            android:exported="true">
            <intent-filter>
                <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
                <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
            </intent-filter>
        </activity>
        
        <!-- Immersive mode -->
        <meta-data android:name="unityplayer.ForwardNativeEventsToDalvik"
            android:value="false" />
    </application>
</manifest>
Adaptive Icons & App Bundles: Android App Bundles (AAB) are the required publishing format. They split your APK into base + configuration APKs (different densities, CPU architectures, languages). This reduces download size by 30-40%. Adaptive icons consist of a foreground layer (200x200dp) and background layer (color or gradient) — the system masks them into various shapes (circle, squircle, rounded square). Generate icons for all densities: mdpi (48x48), hdpi (72x72), xhdpi (96x96), xxhdpi (144x144), xxxhdpi (192x192). Use Android Studio's Image Asset Studio.

# Build Android App Bundle (AAB)
./gradlew bundleRelease

# The AAB is at:
# app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab

# Convert AAB to APK for local testing
java -jar bundletool-all.jar build-apks \
  --bundle=app-release.aab \
  --output=app-release.apks \
  --ks=my-release-key.keystore \
  --ks-pass=pass:password \
  --ks-key-alias=my-alias \
  --key-pass=pass:password

# Install to device (universal APK)
java -jar bundletool-all.jar install-apks \
  --apks=app-release.apks

Xcode & Provisioning: Xcode is required for iOS development. Download from Mac App Store. Create an Apple Developer account ($99/year). Provisioning profiles and certificates authenticate your app: Development certificates (running on test devices), Distribution certificates (App Store), and Push notification certificates. Xcode manages signing automatically with 'Automatically manage signing' — it creates provisioning profiles on-the-fly. For CI, export signing certificates and provisioning profiles as files. Use fastlane match to sync signing across your team.

# Fastlane setup for iOS signing
# Gemfile
source "https://rubygems.org"
gem "fastlane"

# Fastfile
lane :build do
  match(type: "appstore", readonly: true)
  
  build_app(
    workspace: "MyGame.xcworkspace",
    scheme: "MyGame",
    configuration: "Release",
    export_method: "app-store",
    include_bitcode: true,
    include_on_demand_resources: true
  )
  
  upload_to_app_store(
    skip_metadata: true,
    skip_screenshots: true
  )
end

# Run
fastlane build

TestFlight & App Store Connect: App Store Connect manages app metadata, builds, pricing, and releases. Upload builds via Xcode Archive or Transporter app. TestFlight enables internal testing (up to 100 testers, no review) and external testing (up to 10,000 testers, requires Beta App Review). Manage versions with build numbers — each uploaded build increments. Set 'What's New' text per version. Use phased releases (7-day gradual rollout) to catch issues. Monitor crash reports and ratings in App Store Connect Analytics.

# Upload to TestFlight via altool
xcrun altool --upload-app \
  -f MyGame.ipa \
  -t ios \
  -u developer@example.com \
  -p @keychain:AC_PASSWORD

# Or use Transporter CLI
xcrun iTMSTransporter \
  -m upload \
  -f /path/to/ipa \
  -u developer@example.com \
  -p @keychain:AC_PASSWORD

# Fastlane beta deployment
lane :beta do
  match(type: "development")
  build_app(scheme: "MyGame", export_method: "development")
  upload_to_testflight(
    skip_waiting_for_build_processing: true,
    groups: ["Internal Testers", "QA Team"]
  )
end

React Native Deep Dive: React Native enables cross-platform iOS/Android development with React. JavaScript thread runs JS code, while native threads handle UI rendering. The bridge (or JSI in new architecture) communicates between JS and native. Key concepts: Virtual DOM diffing for native views, Flexbox layout (converted to Yoga), Metro bundler for JS bundling, and Hermes JS engine for Android. Performance optimization: use FlatList instead of ScrollView, NativeDriver for animations, useMemo/useCallback for render optimization, and avoid bridge bottlenecks. New Architecture (Fabric + TurboModules) improves performance with synchronous native calls and better interop.
Flutter & Dart Ecosystem: Flutter uses Dart and compiles to native ARM code via Skia/Impeller rendering engine. No JS bridge — framework paints directly to canvas for consistent 120fps performance. Key concepts: Widgets (StatelessWidget, StatefulWidget), BuildContext, RenderObjects, Element tree, and InheritedWidget for state propagation. State management: Provider, Riverpod, Bloc, or GetX. Flutter's widget tree rebuilds on setState, but const constructors and RepaintBoundary optimize rendering. Platform channels communicate with native (MethodChannel, EventChannel, BasicMessageChannel). Impeller engine (replacing Skia in newer versions) reduces jank.
Mobile App Testing Strategies: Mobile testing covers unit tests (business logic), widget/component tests (UI rendering), integration tests (multi-screen flows), and E2E tests (real device/simulator). Tools: Jest/Vitest (RN unit), flutter_test (Flutter unit), Detox (RN E2E), Patrol (Flutter E2E), Maestro (cross-platform E2E), and Firebase Test Lab (device farm). Physical device testing catches real-world issues: notch cutouts, gesture conflicts, keyboard handling, and thermal throttling. Test on multiple OS versions and screen sizes. CI/CD integration with GitHub Actions or Bitrise for automated device testing.

App Store Connect & Google Play Console: App Store deployment involves Apple App Store Connect and Google Play Console. iOS requires: Apple Developer Program ($99/year), code signing certificates, provisioning profiles, and App Store Connect app record. Android requires: Google Play Console account ($25 one-time), keystore for signing, and app signing by Google Play. Key metadata: app icon (multiple sizes), screenshots (various devices), description, keywords, privacy policy URL, and age rating. In-app purchases and subscriptions use StoreKit (iOS) and Billing Library (Android). TestFlight (iOS) and internal testing tracks (Android) enable pre-release distribution.

# Fastlane deployment configuration
# fastlane/Fastfile
lane :deploy_ios do |options|
  match(type: "appstore", readonly: true)
  
  increment_build_number(
    build_number: options[:build_number] || latest_testflight_build_number + 1
  )
  
  build_app(
    scheme: "MyApp",
    workspace: "MyApp.xcworkspace",
    export_method: "app-store"
  )
  
  upload_to_testflight(
    skip_waiting_for_build_processing: false,
    notify_external_testers: true,
    groups: ["Beta Testers"]
  )
  
  # Submit for App Store review
  upload_to_app_store(
    skip_metadata: false,
    skip_screenshots: false,
    submit_for_review: false,
    automatic_release: false,
    phased_release: true
  )
end

lane :deploy_android do
  gradle(task: "bundleRelease")
  
  upload_to_play_store(
    track: "production",
    release_status: "draft",
    json_key: "play-store-credentials.json",
    metadata_path: "fastlane/metadata/android"
  )
end

Code Push & Over-the-Air Updates: Over-the-air (OTA) updates push JS bundle/asset changes without App Store review. React Native: CodePush (Microsoft App Center) or EAS Update (Expo). Flutter: Shorebird Code Push. OTA updates work only for JS/bundle changes, not native code (Swift/Kotlin/Java/ObjC). Native changes require full app store submission. Strategy: OTA for bug fixes and UI tweaks, app store for major features and security updates. Rollback mechanisms: push a previous bundle version or use feature flags to disable problematic features. EAS Update supports branches and channels for staged rollouts.

On-Device ML (CoreML/TFLite/MLX): On-device ML runs models directly on the device for privacy, offline use, and low latency. iOS: CoreML with Neural Engine acceleration. Android: TensorFlow Lite (TFLite) with GPU/NNAPI delegates and ML Kit for common tasks. Apple's MLX framework provides ML research capabilities on Apple Silicon. Model formats: CoreML (.mlpackage), TFLite (.tflite), and MLX (.safetensors). Convert models from PyTorch/TensorFlow using coremltools or TFLite Converter. Quantization (FP16, INT8) reduces model size 2-4x with minimal accuracy loss. Use benchmarks like MLPerf Mobile to compare device performance.
Mobile AR & VR Development: Mobile AR/VR uses device cameras, sensors, and GPUs for immersive experiences. Apple ARKit (iOS) and Google ARCore (Android) provide motion tracking, environmental understanding, and light estimation. Unity's AR Foundation provides cross-platform abstraction. Key concepts: world tracking (6DoF), plane detection, image tracking, object scanning, and people occlusion. Reality Composer Pro (Apple) and Sceneform (Google) simplify 3D asset creation. Performance: use LODs, occlusion culling, reduce draw calls, and target 60fps minimum. Apple Vision Pro brings spatial computing with visionOS.
Mobile Performance Profiling: Mobile performance profiling identifies bottlenecks: slow UI rendering, memory leaks, network latency, and battery drain. iOS: Instruments (Time Profiler, Allocations, Leaks, Energy Log), Xcode Organizer for crash/energy data. Android: Android Studio Profiler (CPU, Memory, Network, Energy), Perfetto for system tracing, and Firebase Performance Monitoring for production. Key metrics: FPS (target 60/120), frame drop rate, launch time (cold/warm/hot), APK/IPA size, memory usage (resident/pss), and ANR (Application Not Responding) rate. Profile on lowest-spec target device, not your flagship.
